title: Indian Students Are Turning Away From US Universities. Here's Where They're Going
excerpt: A new DHS rule capping student visas at four years is the latest blow to Indian enrollment in America, accelerating a shift toward Germany, Ireland, and other alternatives that was already well underway.
body:
• The Trump administration's new DHS rule caps student and exchange visas at four years, cuts post-completion grace periods from 60 to 30 days, and bars graduate students from switching majors or transferring without federal approval.
  • Indian student departures to the US fell 13% in 2024, and F-1 visa issuances dropped 69% during peak months in 2025.
  • An IDP Education survey from early 2026 found the US has slipped to third-choice destination (14% preference), behind Australia (31%) and the UK (19%).
  • Germany, Ireland, and Singapore are absorbing the shift, with German enrollment of Indian students up 105% since 2020.

The Department of Homeland Security published a final rule on July 16 that imposes a four-year cap on F-1 student visas and J-1 exchange visas, ending the decades-old "duration of status" system that let international students remain in the US for as long as their programme required. The rule, effective 60 days after Federal Register publication, also halves the post-graduation grace period from 60 to 30 days and prohibits graduate students from changing their educational objective or transferring institutions without prior DHS authorisation.

For the 363,019 Indian students enrolled in US colleges during 2024–25 — roughly 31% of all international students, according to the Open Doors 2025 report — the rule adds bureaucratic uncertainty to a destination already losing ground.

A Shift Already in Motion

The DHS rule did not create the exodus. According to India's Ministry of External Affairs, Indian nationals departing for US study fell 13% in 2024, from 234,473 to 204,058. F-1 visa issuances to Indian students plummeted 69% during June and July 2025. Visa interviews were suspended for nearly a month in May 2025, and thousands of student visas were revoked.

An IDP Education survey of 5,800 students, conducted between March and April 2026, found the US has dropped to third-most-preferred destination at 14% preference — an eight-point decline from February 2025. Australia leads at 31%, followed by the UK at 19%.

"International students, many of whom will have spent years in the USA, will now have just 30 days to find an employer to sponsor them or immediately be turned into illegal immigrants. Have these people no understanding of how life works?"

— David J. Bier, Director of Immigration Studies, Cato Institute

Where the Students Are Going

Germany has emerged as the biggest beneficiary. Indian enrollment surged from 28,905 in 2020 to 59,419 in 2024 — a 105% increase tracked by DAAD, the German Academic Exchange Service. MEA data shows Germany-bound Indian students grew 49% in a single year. The draw: zero tuition at most public universities, an 18-month post-graduation job-seeker visa, and a total annual cost of ₹15–16 lakh including living expenses — a fraction of the ₹50–80 lakh a US STEM master's degree costs in tuition alone.

Ireland is attracting Indian students in tech and pharma with a two-year post-study work visa and hosting the European headquarters of Google, Meta, Apple, and Microsoft. Singapore and the Netherlands are gaining ground for English-taught programmes at globally ranked institutions.

What the New Rule Changes

Students already in the US will have their stay capped at four years from the effective date. Those in programmes exceeding four years — common in PhD tracks — must apply to USCIS for extensions, shifting the decision from universities to the federal government.

"This final rule ensures that foreign students remain focused on their primary purpose: completing their studies and returning home."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

Critics, including former DHS official Doug Rand, called the rule counterproductive. Universities argue that students are already tracked through the SEVIS system and that added bureaucracy will drive talent to competitors.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the implications extend beyond enrollment numbers. The pipeline of students through American universities has historically fed the H-1B workforce, founded startups, and sustained community institutions. A sustained enrollment decline reshapes the renewal of Indian-American communities in college towns and tech hubs across the country — and with four-year caps, 30-day exit windows, and falling approval rates now the norm, Indian families are directing their tuition money toward destinations that want them.
